arXiv:2605.00229v1 [stat.ML] 30 Apr 2026

A unified perspective on fine-tuning and sampling with diffusion and flow models

Carles Domingo-Enrich    Yuanqi Du Affiliation: Microsoft Research New England Email: {carlesd,yuanqidu}@microsoft.com    Michael S. Albergo Affiliation: Harvard University, Kempner Institute Email: malbergo@fas.harvard.edu
Abstract

We study the problem of training diffusion and flow generative models to sample from target distributions defined by an exponential tilting of a base density; a formulation that subsumes both sampling from unnormalized densities and reward fine-tuning of pre-trained models. This problem can be approached from a stochastic optimal control (SOC) perspective, using adjoint-based or score matching methods, or from a non-equilibrium thermodynamics perspective. We provide a unified framework encompassing these approaches and make three main contributions: (i) bias-variance decompositions revealing that Adjoint Matching/Sampling and Novel Score Matching have finite gradient variance, while Target and Conditional Score Matching do not; (ii) norm bounds on the lean adjoint ODE that theoretically support the effectiveness of adjoint-based methods; and (iii) adaptations of the CMCD and NETS loss functions, along with novel Crooks and Jarzynski identities, to the exponential tilting setting. We validate our analysis with reward fine-tuning experiments on Stable Diffusion 1.5 and 3.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in generative modeling have demonstrated the effectiveness of diffusion and flow matching models for learning complex data distributions (Song et al., 2021; Ho et al., 2020; Lipman et al., 2022; Albergo et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). In many applications, however, it is desirable to tailor the generative process to favor certain qualities, either by sampling from an unnormalized target distribution or by fine-tuning a pre-trained model with a reward function (Uehara et al., 2024; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025; Zhang and Chen, 2022; Holdijk et al., 2023). A natural way to address these challenges is via exponential tilting, wherein a base density is modified to a target one by reweighting with an exponential factor. This formulation not only unifies reward fine-tuning and sampling from unnormalized distributions but also naturally lends itself to analysis using tools from stochastic optimal control (SOC), partial differential equation (PDE) analysis, stochastic processes and thermodynamics.

Motivated by the broad applications, such as text-to-image generation (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) and protein design (Wang et al., 2025), a growing body of work has explored methods for fine-tuning diffusion and flow models. Although the underlying problem structure aligns well with SOC, particularly when cast as controlling an SDE with a reward function, the key challenge is the bias introduced by lifting the base process with the reward function. Uehara et al. (2024) tackled this challenge by solving two SOC problems. Adjoint matching (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) leveraged memoryless noise schedule to bypass this issue and generalized SOC to fine-tune flow models. Moreover, reinforcement learning (RL)-based approaches have also been largely explored (Black et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2025).

In a parallel literature, training diffusion and flow models to sample from unnormalized densities has also been largely studied. Early work (Zhang and Chen, 2022; Vargas et al., 2023; Berner et al., 2022) can be viewed as solving an SOC problem where the reward function is related to the unnormalized density. Another branch of work (Phillips et al., 2024; Akhound-Sadegh et al., 2024) extended the score matching framework with the target score instead of the conditional score. The idea of adjoint matching has also been applied to this problem, together with reciprocal projection for efficient off-policy training (Havens et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a). Moreover, Vargas et al. (2024); Zhong et al. (2024); Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden (2025) leveraged fundamental ideas from non-equilibrium thermodynamics, extending the classical annealed importance sampling (AIS) and Jarzynski equality perspective using path-space variational inference and PDE formulations.

In this paper, we provide a unifying framework that formulates training diffusion and flow models to sample from an exponentially tilted target distribution, which covers reward-based fine-tuning of a pretrained model, as well as sampling from unnormalized densities. Our main contributions are as follows: (i) we derive bias-variance decompositions for adjoint-based and score matching algorithms to compare the algorithms on equal footing, under which AM/AS and Novel Score Matching (NSM, Phillips et al. (2024)) perform favorably; (ii) we bound the norm of the lean adjoint ODE for Adjoint Matching and Sampling (AM/AS), supporting the empirical performance of the algorithms; (iii) we adapt the thermodynamic framework of Vargas et al. (2024) and Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden (2025) to the exponential tilting problem which yields analogs of the Controlled Monte Carlo Diffusions (CMCD) and Non-Equilibrium Transport Sampler (NETS) loss functions, as well as novel variants of the celebrated Crooks fluctuation theorem and Jarzynski equality. Finally, we perform reward-based fine-tuning experiments on Stable Diffusion 1.5 and 3 using Adjoint Matching, refining the techniques of Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025).

2 Background

2.1 Flow Matching, DDIM and Föllmer processes

Flow Matching or Stochastic Interpolants

Given a real-valued differentiable function (αt)t∈[0,1](\alpha_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} such that α0=0\alpha_{0}=0, α1=1\alpha_{1}=1, and a real-valued differentiable function (βt)t∈[0,1](\beta_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} such that β1=0\beta_{1}=0, the reference flow or stochastic interpolant X¯\bar{X} is defined as

X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε,\textstyle\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon, (1)

where ε∼p0=𝒩⁡(0,I)\varepsilon\sim p_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{I}), Y∼pdataY\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. If we let

κt=α˙tαt,ηt=βt​(α˙tαt​βt−β˙t),\textstyle\kappa_{t}=\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}},\qquad\eta_{t}=\beta_{t}\big(\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\beta_{t}-\dot{\beta}_{t}\big), (2)

the Flow Matching reference SDE, whose solution has the same time marginals as the reference flow up to a time flip, is

d​X~t\textstyle d\tilde{X}_{t} =−κ1−t​X~t​d​t+2​η1−t​d​Bt,X~0∼pdata.\textstyle=-\kappa_{1-t}\tilde{X}_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\eta_{1-t}}\,\mathrm{d}B_{t},\qquad\tilde{X}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. (3)

That is, for all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], X~t\tilde{X}_{t} and X¯1−t\bar{X}_{1-t} have the same distribution. And the optimal generative SDE reads

d​Xt\textstyle dX_{t} =(κt​Xt+(σ​(t)22+ηt)​𝔰t​(Xt))​d​t+σ⁡(t)​d​Bt,X0∼𝒩⁡(0,β02​I),\textstyle=\big(\kappa_{t}X_{t}+\big(\frac{\sigma(t)^{2}}{2}+\eta_{t}\big)\mathfrak{s}_{t}(X_{t})\big)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(t)\,\mathrm{d}B_{t},\qquad X_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{0}^{2}\mathrm{I}), (4)

where 𝔰t\mathfrak{s}_{t} is the score function of the reference process: 𝔰t​(x)=∇log⁡pt​(x)\mathfrak{s}_{t}(x)=\nabla\log p_{t}(x), and the noise schedule σ\sigma is arbitrary. For any σ\sigma, the marginals XtX_{t} also have the same distribution as the reference flow marginals X¯t\bar{X}_{t}. Setting σ⁡(t)=2​ηt\sigma(t)=\sqrt{2\eta_{t}} yields the memoryless process, which is the time reversal of the process in (3):

d​Xt\textstyle dX_{t} =(κt​Xt+2​ηt​𝔰t​(Xt))​d​t+2​ηt​d​Bt,X0∼𝒩⁡(0,β02​I).\textstyle=\big(\kappa_{t}X_{t}+2\eta_{t}\mathfrak{s}_{t}(X_{t})\big)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}B_{t},\qquad X_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{0}^{2}\mathrm{I}). (5)
Remark 2.1.

Although the drift terms in (4) and (5) are written in terms of the score to facilitate the analysis, in Flow Matching the vector field that is learned is vt​(x)=κt​Xt+ηt​𝔰t​(x)v_{t}(x)=\kappa_{t}X_{t}+\eta_{t}\mathfrak{s}_{t}(x), and in DDIM it is often the noise predictor ϵt​(x)=−βt​𝔰t​(x)\epsilon_{t}(x)=-\beta_{t}\mathfrak{s}_{t}(x). These vector fields encode the same information, and the drifts can be written in terms of any of them.

Subcases of Flow Matching

The following processes are particular instances of flow matching:

  1. (i)

    Föllmer process: Given an increasing function α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} such that α¯0=0\bar{\alpha}_{0}=0 and α¯1=1\bar{\alpha}_{1}=1, and a constant σ02>0\sigma_{0}^{2}>0, the interpolant X¯\bar{X} and the coefficients αt\alpha_{t}, βt\beta_{t}, κt\kappa_{t} and ηt\eta_{t} read

    X¯t=α¯tY+α¯t​(1−α¯t)σ0ε⟹αt=α¯t,βt=α¯t​(1−α¯t)σ0,α˙t=α¯˙t,β˙t=(1−2​α¯t)​α¯˙t2​α¯t​(1−α¯t)σ02,⟹κt=α¯˙tα¯t,ηt=α¯˙t​σ022.\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\bar{X}_{t}=\bar{\alpha}_{t}Y+\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})}\sigma_{0}\varepsilon\implies\alpha_{t}=\bar{\alpha}_{t},\quad\beta_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})}\sigma_{0},\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\dot{\alpha}_{t}=\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t},\quad\dot{\beta}_{t}=\frac{(1-2\bar{\alpha}_{t})\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}}{2\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})}}\sigma_{0}^{2},\implies\kappa_{t}=\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}},\quad\eta_{t}=\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2}.\end{split} (6)
  2. (ii)

    DDIM/DDPM: Given an increasing function α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} such that α¯0=0\bar{\alpha}_{0}=0 and α¯1=1\bar{\alpha}_{1}=1, and a constant σ02>0\sigma_{0}^{2}>0, the interpolants and coefficients αt\alpha_{t}, βt\beta_{t}, κt\kappa_{t} and ηt\eta_{t} read

    X¯t=α¯tY+1−α¯tσ0ε⟹αt=α¯t,βt=1−α¯tσ0,α˙t=α¯˙t2​α¯t,β˙t=−α¯˙t2​1−α¯tσ0,⟹κt=α¯˙t2​α¯t,ηt=α¯˙t​σ022​α¯t.\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\bar{X}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}Y+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\sigma_{0}\varepsilon\implies\alpha_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}},\quad\beta_{t}=\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\sigma_{0},\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\dot{\alpha}_{t}=\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}}{2\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}},\quad\dot{\beta}_{t}=-\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}}{2\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\sigma_{0},\implies\kappa_{t}=\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}}{2\bar{\alpha}_{t}},\quad\eta_{t}=\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2\bar{\alpha}_{t}}.\end{split} (7)
  3. (iii)

    Rectified Flow (OT Flow Matching): Given an increasing function α¯t\bar{\alpha}_{t} such that α¯0=0\bar{\alpha}_{0}=0 and α¯1=1\bar{\alpha}_{1}=1, and a constant σ02>0\sigma_{0}^{2}>0, the interpolant X¯\bar{X} and the coefficients αt\alpha_{t}, βt\beta_{t}, κt\kappa_{t} and ηt\eta_{t} read

    X¯t=α¯tY+(1−α¯t)σ0ε⟹αt=α¯t,βt=(1−α¯t)σ0.α˙t=α¯˙t,β˙t=−α¯˙t,⟹κt=α¯˙tα¯t,ηt=(1−α¯t)​α¯˙t​σ02α¯t.\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\bar{X}_{t}=\bar{\alpha}_{t}Y+(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sigma_{0}\varepsilon\implies\alpha_{t}=\bar{\alpha}_{t},\quad\beta_{t}=(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sigma_{0}.\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\dot{\alpha}_{t}=\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t},\quad\dot{\beta}_{t}=-\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t},\implies\kappa_{t}=\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}},\quad\eta_{t}=\frac{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}.\end{split} (8)

2.2 Exponential tilting and its control and thermodynamic formulations

The exponential tilting problem

Given a Flow Matching model that generates a distribution pbasep^{\mathrm{base}} over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and a function r:ℝd→ℝr:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}, consider the task of modifying the model such that the generated distribution is the following tilted distribution:

p⋆​(x)∝pbase​(x)​exp⁡(r⁡(x)).\textstyle p^{\star}(x)\propto p^{\mathrm{base}}(x)\exp(r(x)). (9)

Two main settings are covered by the exponential tilting framework:

  1. (i)

    Reward fine-tuning: pbasep^{\mathrm{base}} is the distribution generated by a pre-trained diffusion or flow matching model, and rr is a reward model that takes high values for high quality samples.

  2. (ii)

    Sampling from unnormalized distributions: The goal is to sample from the unnormalized distribution proportional to p⋆​(x)=exp⁡(−E⁡(x))p^{\star}(x)=\exp(-E(x)), where EE is the energy function. pbasep^{\mathrm{base}} is a Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,σ12​I)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{1}^{2}\mathrm{I}), and the reward rr is chosen to be r⁡(x)=−E⁡(x)+‖x‖22​σ12r(x)=-E(x)+\frac{\|x\|^{2}}{2\sigma_{1}^{2}}.

While the Föllmer process is typically used for sampling (e.g. Havens et al. (2025)), and DDIM and OT Flow Matching are commonly used for generative modeling, the choice of process is independent of the application.

The stochastic optimal control formulation

Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025) proves that the exponential tilting problem can be reformulated as the following stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem:11 1 In (12), 𝔰t\mathfrak{s}_{t} is the score function corresponding to pbasep^{\mathrm{base}}. In practice, bσb_{\sigma} is computed using the learned FM vector field or denoiser (Rem. 2.1).

minu∈𝒰⁡𝔼⁡[12​∫01‖u⁡(Xtu,t)‖2​𝑑t+g⁡(X1u)],\textstyle\min\limits_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|u(X^{u}_{t},t)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t+g(X^{u}_{1})\big], (10)
s.t.dXut=(bσ(Xut,t)+σ(t)u(Xut,t))dt+σ(t)dBt,Xu0∼p0=𝒩(0,β02I),\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\text{s.t.}~\mathrm{d}X^{u}_{t}=\left(b_{\sigma}(X^{u}_{t},t)+\sigma(t)u(X^{u}_{t},t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(t)\mathrm{d}B_{t},\qquad X^{u}_{0}\sim p_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{0}^{2}\mathrm{I}),\end{split} (11)
wherebσ​(x,t)=κt​x+(σ​(t)22+ηt)​𝔰t​(x),\textstyle\text{where}\quad b_{\sigma}(x,t)=\kappa_{t}x+\big(\frac{\sigma(t)^{2}}{2}+\eta_{t}\big)\mathfrak{s}_{t}(x), (12)

as long as the uncontrolled process X=X0X=X^{0} satisfies the memoryless property, meaning that X0X_{0} and X1X_{1} are statistically independent. (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025, Prop. 1) shows that a generative process is memoryless if and only if the noise schedule is chosen as σ​(t)2=2​ηt+χ⁡(t)\sigma(t)^{2}=2\eta_{t}+\chi(t), with χ:[0,1]→ℝ\chi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} such that for all t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1], limt′→0+αt′exp(−∫t′tχ⁡(s)2​βs2ds)=0\lim_{t^{\prime}\to 0^{+}}\alpha_{t^{\prime}}\exp\big(-\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}\frac{\chi(s)}{2\beta_{s}^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)=0. In particular, they refer to σ⁡(t)=2​ηt\sigma(t)=\sqrt{2\eta_{t}} as the memoryless noise schedule, as it is the only one such that the resulting fine-tuned model can be used to perform inference with an arbitrary noise schedule (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025, Thm. 1).

The thermodynamics formulation

Methods like CMCD (Vargas et al., 2024) and NETS (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2025) were developed in a setting where one has access to a time-dependent energy function (Ut)t∈[0,1](U_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}, instead of a flow matching vector field that generates pbasep_{\mathrm{base}} and a time-dependent reward function (rt)t∈[0,1](r_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}. That is, their goal is to learn a vector field that yields a process with marginals pt⋆​(x)∝exp⁡(−Ut​(x))p^{\star}_{t}(x)\propto\exp(-U_{t}(x)). This is different but related to the task of learning a vector field that yields a process with marginals pt⋆​(x)∝ptbase​(x)​exp⁡(rt​(x))p^{\star}_{t}(x)\propto p^{\mathrm{base}}_{t}(x)\exp(r_{t}(x)), which solves the exponential tilting problem (9) if (rt)t∈[0,1](r_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} is chosen such that r1=rr_{1}=r and p0⋆∝𝒩⁡(0,β02)​exp⁡(r0)p^{\star}_{0}\propto\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{0}^{2})\exp(r_{0}) is easy to sample from. More specifically, we consider processes XvX^{v} of the form

dXtv=(bσr(Xtv,t)+v(Xtv,t))dt+σ(t)dBt,{X0v∼p0⋆∝𝒩⁡(0,β02​I)​exp⁡(r0),bσr​(x,t):=κt​x+(σ​(t)22+ηt)​(𝔰t​(x)+∇rt​(x)).\textstyle\mathrm{d}X^{v}_{t}=\left(b^{r}_{\sigma}(X^{v}_{t},t)+v(X^{v}_{t},t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(t)\mathrm{d}B_{t},\quad\begin{cases}X^{v}_{0}\sim p^{\star}_{0}\propto\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{0}^{2}\mathrm{I})\exp(r_{0}),\\ b^{r}_{\sigma}(x,t)\!:=\!\kappa_{t}x\!+\!\big(\frac{\sigma(t)^{2}}{2}\!+\!\eta_{t}\big)\big(\mathfrak{s}_{t}(x)\!+\!\nabla r_{t}(x)\big).\end{cases} (13)

and our goal is to learn a v⋆v^{\star} such that the marginal distribution of Xtv⋆X^{v^{\star}}_{t} is pt⋆​(x)∝ptbase​(x)​exp⁡(rt​(x))p^{\star}_{t}(x)\propto p^{\mathrm{base}}_{t}(x)\exp(r_{t}(x)). Unlike in the SOC formulation, in the thermodynamics formulation the noise schedule σ⁡(t)\sigma(t) can be picked arbitrarily.

3 Stochastic optimal control algorithms and analysis

3.1 Adjoint-based methods

Adjoint Matching

Adjoint Matching (AM) is a SOC deep learning loss introduced by Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025). For the exponential tilting problem with scalar σ\sigma, it takes the following form:

ℒAdj−Match(u;Xu¯):=12∫01∥\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Adj-Match}}(u;X^{\bar{u}}):=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\| u(Xtu¯,t)+σ(t)a~(t;Xu¯)∥2dt,u¯=stopgrad(u),\textstyle u(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)+\sigma(t)\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t,\qquad\bar{u}=\texttt{stopgrad}(u), (14)
where dd​t​a~​(t,Xu¯)\textstyle\text{where }\quad\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}}) =−∇xbσ​(Xtu¯,t)⊤​a~​(t,Xu¯),\textstyle=-\nabla_{x}b_{\sigma}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)^{\top}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}}), (15)
a~​(1,Xu¯)\textstyle\tilde{a}(1;X^{\bar{u}}) =−∇xr​(X1u¯).\textstyle=-\nabla_{x}r(X^{\bar{u}}_{1}). (16)

Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025) refer to the ODE (15)-(16) as the lean adjoint ODE. They show that if uu is a critical point of the expected loss ℒAdj−Match​(u):=𝔼⁡[ℒAdj−Match​(u,Xu¯)]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Adj-Match}}(u):=\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Adj-Match}}(u;X^{\bar{u}})] that is, if δδ​u​ℒAdj−Match​(u)≡0\frac{\delta}{\delta u}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Adj-Match}}(u)\equiv 0, then uu is the optimal control u⋆u^{\star}.

Adjoint Sampling

Adjoint Sampling was introduced by Havens et al. (2025) as a procedure based on Adjoint Matching to sample from unnormalized densities, with improved efficiency. When pbasep^{\mathrm{base}} is a Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,σ12​I)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{1}^{2}\mathrm{I}), we have that X¯t∼𝒩⁡(0,(αt2​σ12+βt2)​I)\bar{X}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,(\alpha^{2}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2})\mathrm{I}), which means that b⁡(x,t)b(x,t) defined in (12) is a linear function of xx: bσ​(x,t)=(κt−σ​(t)2+2​ηt2​(αt2​σ12+βt2))​x:=χt​xb_{\sigma}(x,t)=\big(\kappa_{t}-\frac{\sigma(t)^{2}+2\eta_{t}}{2(\alpha^{2}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2})}\big)x:=\chi_{t}x. Hence, the adjoint ODE (15) needs not be solved as it admits a closed form solution: a~​(t,Xu¯)=−exp⁡(∫t1χs​𝑑s)​∇xr​(X1u¯)\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})=-\exp\big(\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\nabla_{x}r(X^{\bar{u}}_{1}). To obtain a further speed-up, in Adjoint Sampling the loss is not evaluated at intermediate points of the trajectory Xu¯X^{\bar{u}}, but rather at points X¯tu¯=αt​X1u¯+βt​ε\bar{X}^{\bar{u}}_{t}=\alpha_{t}X^{\bar{u}}_{1}+\beta_{t}\varepsilon obtained by noising the final iterate X1u¯X^{\bar{u}}_{1}:

ℒAdj−Sampl(u):=𝔼X¯tu¯=αt​X1u¯+βt​ε[12∫01∥\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Adj-Sampl}}(u):=\mathbb{E}_{\bar{X}^{\bar{u}}_{t}=\alpha_{t}X^{\bar{u}}_{1}+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\| u(X¯tu¯,t)−exp(∫t1χsds)σ(t)∇xr(X1u¯)∥2dt]\textstyle u(\bar{X}^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)\!-\!\exp\big(\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\sigma(t)\nabla_{x}r(X^{\bar{u}}_{1})\big\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big] (17)

Each rollout X1u¯X^{\bar{u}}_{1} can be noised multiple times, which yields an algorithm that is much more efficient than AM, even though it is more restrictive because it only works for sampling.

The behavior of Adjoint Matching and Sampling depends heavily on the norm of the solution to the lean adjoint ODE. In the following proposition we bound the norm of a~​(t,Xu¯)\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}}) under convexity assumptions on pbasep^{\mathrm{base}}.

Proposition 3.1 (Norm of the lean adjoint state).

Let a~​(t,Xu)\tilde{a}(t,X^{u}) be the solution of the lean adjoint ODE (15)-(16) with memoryless schedule σ⁡(t)=2​ηt\sigma(t)=\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}. Assume there exists σ12>0\sigma_{1}^{2}>0 such that the density pbasep^{\mathrm{base}} is 1σ12\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}-strongly log-concave, i.e. −∇2​log​pbase​(x)⪰1σ12​I-\nabla^{2}\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(x)\succeq\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}\mathrm{I}. Let χt:=κt−2​ηtβt2+αt2​σ12\chi_{t}:=\kappa_{t}-\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\beta^{2}_{t}+\alpha^{2}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}}. For all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], we have that

‖a~​(t,Xu)‖≤exp⁡(∫t1χs​𝑑s)​‖∇xr​(X1u)‖.\textstyle\|\tilde{a}(t,X^{u})\|\leq\exp\big(\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\|\nabla_{x}r(X^{u}_{1})\|. (18)

In particular, (i) for the Föllmer schedule, exp⁡(∫t1χs​𝑑s)=σ12(1−α¯t)​σ02+α¯t​σ12\exp\big(\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)=\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sigma_{0}^{2}+\bar{\alpha}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}}, (ii) for DDPM/DDIM, exp⁡(∫t1χs​𝑑s)=σ12​α¯t(1−α¯t)​σ02+α¯t​σ12\exp\big(\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)=\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sigma_{0}^{2}+\bar{\alpha}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}}, and (iii) for Rectified Flow, exp⁡(∫t1χs​𝑑s)=α¯t(1−α¯t)2+α¯t2\exp\big(\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)=\frac{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})^{2}+\bar{\alpha}^{2}_{t}}. Moreover, when pbase=𝒩⁡(0,σ12​I)p^{\mathrm{base}}=\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{1}^{2}\mathrm{I}) as in Adjoint Sampling, equation (18) holds with equality.

The proof of Prop. 3.1 in Sec. B.1 relies on bounding the spectrum of Sym⁡(∇bσ)\mathrm{Sym}(\nabla b_{\sigma}), which is connected to the spectrum of ∇2​log​pbase\nabla^{2}\log p^{\mathrm{base}}. While strong convexity of pbasep^{\mathrm{base}} is a strong condition in the fine-tuning case, since spectra are local properties, as long as the trajectory Xu¯X^{\bar{u}} spends most of the time t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] in regions where ptbasep^{\mathrm{base}}_{t} is locally strongly log-concave (basins of ptbasep^{\mathrm{base}}_{t}), the norm ‖a~​(t,Xu¯)‖\|\tilde{a}(t,X^{\bar{u}})\| will decay accordingly. This explains the norm decay and consequent good performance of the algorithm in realistic settings (Sec. 5).

3.2 Score matching methods

In what follows, we include a review of existing score-based generative modeling methods (see derivations in Sec. B.2). These methods are designed to learn arbitrary distributions pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}; and all require having access to samples from pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} as well as the noiseless score ∇log⁡pdata\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}, except for Conditional Score Matching, which only relies on samples from pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}. These loss functions follow from these three identities involving the score function of the distribution of X¯t\bar{X}_{t} (see Lem. A.1):

​C​o​n​d​i​t​i​o​n​a​l​s​c​o​r​e​i​d​e​n​t​i​t​y:∇log⁡pt​(x)=−∫ℝd(x−αt​y)​𝒩​(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑yβt2​∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y,\textstyle\emph{Conditionalscoreidentity:}\qquad\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=-\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(x-\alpha_{t}y)\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{\beta_{t}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}, (CSI)
​T​a​r​g​e​t​s​c​o​r​e​i​d​e​n​t​i​t​y:∇log⁡pt​(x)=∫ℝd∇log⁡pdata​(y)​𝒩​(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑yαt​∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y.\textstyle\emph{Targetscoreidentity:}\qquad\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{\alpha_{t}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}. (TSI)
​N​o​v​e​l​s​c​o​r​e​i​d​e​n​t​i​t​y:∇log⁡pt​(x)=∫ℝd(αt∇logpdata(y)−(x−αty))𝒩(x;αty,β2tI)pdata(y)dy(αt2+βt2)​∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y\textstyle\emph{Novelscoreidentity:}\qquad\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\alpha_{t}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)-(x-\alpha_{t}y))\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{(\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2})\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y} (NSI)

Observe that (NSI) follows from summing αt2/(αt2+βt2)\alpha_{t}^{2}/(\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}) times (TSI) and βt2/(αt2+βt2)\beta_{t}^{2}/(\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}) times (CSI).

Target Score Matching

The Target Score Matching loss was proposed by (Bortoli et al., 2024), and is a consequence of the target score identity (TSI), and the fact that when pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} is the tilted distribution (9), its score is ∇log⁡pdata=∇log⁡pbase+∇r​(x)\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}=\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{base}}+\nabla r(x). The loss function reads

ℒTSM​(s^)=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)−1αt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))‖2​w​(X¯t,t)​𝑑t],\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TSM}}(\hat{s})\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\\ \bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon\end{subarray}}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)\!-\!\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(Y)\!+\!\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}w(\bar{X}_{t},t)\,\mathrm{d}t\big], (19)

where w:ℝd×[0,1]→(0,+∞)w:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[0,1]\to(0,+\infty) is an arbitrary weight function.

Conditional Score Matching

The well-known Conditional Score Matching loss was used by the foundational works on diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020; Song and Ermon, 2019), and can be derived from the conditional score identity (CSI) analogously to the Target Score Matching loss. In our notation, the loss reads

ℒCSM​(s^)=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)+X¯t−αt​Yβt2‖2​w​(X¯t,t)​𝑑t],\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CSM}}(\hat{s})=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\\ \bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon\end{subarray}}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)+\frac{\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y}{\beta^{2}_{t}}\|^{2}w(\bar{X}_{t},t)\,\mathrm{d}t\big], (20)

where ww is an arbitrary weight function as in equation (119) (see Sec. B.2).

Novel Score Matching

The novel score matching loss was introduced by Phillips et al. (2024), and can be derived from the novel score identity (NSI) analogously to the Target Score Matching loss. The loss function reads:

ℒNSM​(s^)=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)−αt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))−(X¯t−αt​Y)αt2+βt2‖2​w​(X¯t,t)​𝑑t].\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NSM}}(\hat{s})\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\\ \bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon\end{subarray}}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)\!-\!\frac{\alpha_{t}(\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y))-(\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y)}{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}}\|^{2}w(\bar{X}_{t},t)\,\mathrm{d}t\big]. (21)

Iterated Denoising Energy Matching

A fourth loss function which assumes access to the density pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} and thus can only be used for sampling is the iDEM loss (Akhound-Sadegh et al., 2024), defined as

ℒiDEM​(s^)=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε,(εi)i=1n∼𝒩⁡(0,I)​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)−1αt​∑i=1n∇log⁡pdata​(X¯t−βt​εiαt)​pdata​(X¯t−βt​εiαt)∑i=1npdata​(X¯t−βt​εiαt)‖2​𝑑t].\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{iDEM}}(\hat{s})\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\\ \bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon,\\ (\varepsilon_{i})_{i=1}^{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{I})\end{subarray}}\bigg[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)\!-\!\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{\bar{X}_{t}-\beta_{t}\varepsilon_{i}}{\alpha_{t}})p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{\bar{X}_{t}-\beta_{t}\varepsilon_{i}}{\alpha_{t}})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{\bar{X}_{t}-\beta_{t}\varepsilon_{i}}{\alpha_{t}})}\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg]. (22)

It can be viewed as a biased approximation of the quantity

𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)−𝔼⁡[1αt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))|X¯t]‖2​𝑑t],\textstyle\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\,|\,\bar{X}_{t}\big]\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big], (23)

which is equal to the bias term of the Target Score Matching loss (19) (see (25)).

Solving the exponential tilting problem with score-based methods

Naturally, the score-based methods presented above can also be used to sample from the tilted distribution pdata​(x)∝pbase​(x)​exp⁡(r⁡(x))p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\propto p^{\mathrm{base}}(x)\exp(r(x)) provided that we have samples from this distribution, which may be obtained e.g. using SMC methods (Phillips et al., 2024). In practice, the score-based methods that make explicit use of the score ∇log⁡pdata=∇log⁡pbase​(x)+∇r​(x)\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}=\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(x)+\nabla r(x) can be used even when we initially are only able to sample from pbasep^{\mathrm{base}}, as it is expected that if we keep on sampling using the learned model, the generated distribution will converge to the tilted distribution. In fact, some methods such as iDEM are introduced to work on-policy in this fashion. However, there are no theoretical guarantees that the on-policy versions of these algorithms converge to the tilted distribution.

3.3 Algorithm comparison through bias-variance decompositions

In this section, we show that all the loss functions presented in Sec. 3 can be written as the sum of a KL divergence term between a learned process and an optimal process (the bias term), and a positive term that has no contribution to the expected gradient (the variance term). To compare all algorithms on an equal footing, we write the learned fine-tuned generative SDE with memoryless schedule σ⁡(t)=2​ηt\sigma(t)=\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}, i.e. d​Xt=vft​(Xt,t)​d​t+2​ηt​d​BtdX_{t}=v_{\mathrm{ft}}(X_{t},t)\,dt+\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}\,dB_{t}, with X0∼𝒩⁡(0,σ02​I)X_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathrm{I}). We set the importance weights of each loss function such that it takes the form:

ℒ⁡(vft)=𝔼⁡[12​∫01‖vft​(Xt,t)−ξ⁡(t,X)‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t],\textstyle\mathcal{L}(v_{\mathrm{ft}})=\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\|v_{\mathrm{ft}}(X_{t},t)-\xi(t,X)\big\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big], (24)

where the process XX and the vector field ξ\xi depend on the specific algorithm (see Prop. 3.2 and Prop. 3.3). Observe that this general loss can be further rewritten as

ℒ⁡(vft)=𝔼⁡[∫01‖vft​(Xt,t)−𝔼⁡[ξ⁡(t,X)|Xt]‖2​12​ηt​dt]⏟Bias+𝔼⁡[∫01‖ξ⁡(t,X)−𝔼⁡[ξ⁡(t,X)|Xt]‖2​12​ηt​dt]⏟Variance.\textstyle\mathcal{L}(v_{\mathrm{ft}})=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\big\|v_{\mathrm{ft}}(X_{t},t)-\mathbb{E}[\xi(t,X)|X_{t}]\big\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]}_{\mathrm{Bias}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\big\|\xi(t,X)-\mathbb{E}[\xi(t,X)|X_{t}]\big\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]}_{\mathrm{Variance}}. (25)

In certain instances, the bias term equals the (forward or reverse) KL divergence between the path measures of the optimal and learned processes, through the Girsanov theorem. The variance term does not contribute to the expected gradient, but it adds noise to the empirical gradient; it is desirable to minimize its contribution.

Proposition 3.2 (Bias-variance decomposition for Adjoint Matching and Sampling).

The Adjoint Matching and Sampling loss functions in (14) and (17) fit the general form (24) by setting X=Xu¯,X¯u¯X=X^{\bar{u}},\bar{X}^{\bar{u}} resp., and identifying v⁡(x,t)/2​ηt=u⁡(x,t)v(x,t)/\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}=u(x,t), ξ⁡(t,X)/2​ηt=2​ηt​a~​(t,X)\xi(t,X)/\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}=\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}\tilde{a}(t,X). Assume that the density pbasep^{\mathrm{base}} is 1σ12\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}-strongly log-concave, i.e. −∇2​log​pbase​(x)⪰1σ12​I-\nabla^{2}\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(x)\succeq\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}\mathrm{I}. Then,

  1. (i)

    The variance term in (25) admits the upper-bound σ122​𝔼Y∼pbase​[‖∇xr​(Y)‖2]\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{2}\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p^{\mathrm{base}}}[\|\nabla_{x}r(Y)\|^{2}] for three subcases of Flow Matching considered in Sec. 2.1.

  2. (ii)

    If pbase=𝒩⁡(0,σ12​I)p^{\mathrm{base}}=\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{1}^{2}\mathrm{I}) as in AS, the variance term is σ122​Tr​(CovY∼𝒩⁡(0,σ12​I)​[∇xr​(Y)])\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{2}\mathrm{Tr}\big(\mathrm{Cov}_{Y\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{1}^{2}\mathrm{I})}[\nabla_{x}r(Y)]\big).

  3. (iii)

    If we consider the AM loss function in which the expectation is with respect to the optimal process (4), then the bias term is equal to the KL divergence KL(ℙ⋆||ℙu)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}^{\star}||\mathbb{P}^{u}) between the optimal measure and the measure of XuX^{u}.

As we remark in Sec. 3.1, the strong convexity assumption on pbasep^{\mathrm{base}} is strong for the fine-tuning case, but a similar behavior is expected to hold in general. Note the AM loss function with optimal process expectation can be implemented via a Girsanov factor, and was first studied by (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2024, App. C.4) under the name SOCM-Adjoint method. Next, we prove a similar result for score matching methods.

Proposition 3.3 (Bias-variance decomposition for score matching methods).

The Target, Conditional and Novel Score Matching loss functions in (19), (20) and (21) fit the general form (24) by setting X=X¯X=\bar{X} (the reference flow) and weight function w⁡(x,t)=ηtw(x,t)=\eta_{t}, identifying s^​(x,t)=vft​(x,t)−κt​x2​ηt\hat{s}(x,t)=\frac{v_{\mathrm{ft}}(x,t)-\kappa_{t}x}{2\eta_{t}}, and ξ⁡(t,X)=κt​X¯t+2​ηtαt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))\xi(t,X)=\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big), ξ⁡(t,X)=κt​X¯t−2​ηt​(X¯t−αt​Y)βt2\xi(t,X)=\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}-\frac{2\eta_{t}(\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y)}{\beta_{t}^{2}}, and ξ⁡(t,X)=κt​X¯t+2​ηt​(αt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))−(X¯t−αt​Y))αt2+βt2\xi(t,X)=\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}\big(\alpha_{t}(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y))-(\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y)\big)}{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}}, respectively. Moreover,

  1. (i)

    For TSM and CSM, the variance term in (25) is infinite for the three subcases of Flow Matching considered in Sec. 2.1.

  2. (ii)

    For NSM, the variance term admits the bounds shown in Tab. 1 (the bounds have a removable discontinuity at σ0=1\sigma_{0}=1).

  3. (iii)

    For TSM, CSM and NSM, the bias term is equal to the KL divergence KL(ℙ⋆||ℙs^)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}^{\star}||\mathbb{P}^{\hat{s}}) between the optimal measure and the measure of Xs^X^{\hat{s}}, the process induced by s^\hat{s}.

The reason that the variance term is infinite for TSM is that its integrand blows up at t=0t=0, and for CSM it blows up both at t=0t=0 and t=1t=1. Surprisingly, NSM manages to avoid all blow-ups. The infinite variance terms for TSM and CSM means that these methods cannot be run with weight w⁡(x,t)=ηtw(x,t)=\eta_{t}, i.e. by optimizing the expected loss function KL(ℙ⋆||ℙs^)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}^{\star}||\mathbb{P}^{\hat{s}}), as the noise would be infinite (up to numerical aspects). Of course, that does not preclude using different weight functions, but those other weight functions will likely not yield a loss function with a probabilistic interpretation in terms of path measures like w⁡(x,t)=ηtw(x,t)=\eta_{t} does. Lastly, iDEM has a similar behavior to TSM, by the connection that we point out in (23).

In this section, we adapt the methods from (Vargas et al., 2024) and (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2025) to solve the thermodynamics formulation of the exponential tilting problem as described in Sec. 2.2. Relying on similar tools, we also prove novel versions of the escorted Crooks fluctuation theorem and the Jarzynski equality tailored to the exponential tilting dynamics.

5 Experiments

While the scope of our paper is general, as we cover fine-tuning and sampling, and many different algorithms, in this section we focus on the performance of Adjoint Matching for fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 and Stable Diffusion 3 with ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023) as the reward model. We fine-tune using the 10000 prompts considered by Xu et al. (2023) and report metrics computed on their 100-prompt validation dataset (generating 10 images per prompt).

In Fig. 1 we plot the trade-offs Astolfi et al. (2024) between DreamSim variance (Fu et al. (2023), a metric that measures per-prompt diversity) and ImageReward, CLIPScore (Hessel et al., 2021) and HPSv2 (Wu et al., 2023). Our results follow the same trend as those of Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025), which carried out similar experiments on a proprietary base model. We use the η≥0\eta\geq 0 as a multiplier of the noise σ⁡(t)=2​ηt\sigma(t)=\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}: the effective noise is η​σ​(t)\eta\sigma(t) (η\eta and ηt\eta_{t} denote different quantities). We perform inference with η=0\eta=0 (no noise) and η=1\eta=1 (memoryless), and with two schedules: the default DDIM schedule and the schedule used during fine-tuning. Remarkably, η=0\eta=0 performs better w.r.t ImageReward and HPS, and η=1\eta=1 is better at CLIPScore.

In Fig. 2(left) we plot the same trade-offs for Stable Diffusion 3, and include Aesthetic Score (LAION, 2024) as well. Arguably, η=1\eta=1 outperforms η=0\eta=0 in this case, as most points on the Pareto front use the former. In Fig. 2(right) we ablate the choice of the initial variance σ02\sigma_{0}^{2}; as we show in Sec. D.1, we can simulate a generative SDE with a rescaled noise schedule σ\sigma by reusing the pretrained vector field, which was learned at σ02\sigma_{0}^{2}. In the figure, points linked by an arrow correspond to settings which only differ by the training σ02\sigma_{0}^{2}, the tail being for σ02=1\sigma_{0}^{2}=1 and the head being for σ02=1.5\sigma_{0}^{2}=1.5. We perform inference at both σ02=1\sigma_{0}^{2}=1 and 1.5. The results are inconclusive, which is consistent with Prop. 3.2, that states that the (bound on the) variance term for Adjoint Matching is independent of σ0\sigma_{0}.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced new developments that clarify the algorithmic design of fine-tuning and sampling in diffusion and flow models, and validated key implications with empirical studies. Together, our results help unify seemingly disparate procedures within a common perspective and suggest principled routes for designing improved algorithms.

Limitations and future work. Our experiments focused on fine-tuning text-to-image diffusion models. Extending the empirical evaluation to other domains such as protein design remains future work. In addition, we primarily evaluated SOC- and score matching approaches, and leave a systematic study of the proposed thermodynamics-inspired methods for future investigation. Finally, our framework is not comprehensive: it does not explicitly include several recent fine-tuning and sampling algorithms (e.g., Liu et al. (2025b); Akhound-Sadegh et al. (2025)), which we view as an important direction for extending the scope of the analysis.

Lemma A.1 (Conditional and target score identities, Bortoli et al. (2024)).

We write the density of the Gaussian 𝒩⁡(αt​y,βt2​I)\mathcal{N}(\alpha_{t}y,\beta_{t}^{2}\mathrm{I}) as 𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)=exp⁡(−‖x−αt​y‖22​βt2)/(2​π​βt2)d/2\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta_{t}^{2}\mathrm{I})=\exp\big(-\frac{\|x-\alpha_{t}y\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)/(2\pi\beta^{2}_{t})^{d/2}. Then,

pt​(x)=∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y=[(Tαt)#​pdata∗𝒩⁡(0,βt2​I)]​(x),\textstyle p_{t}(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y=[(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}\ast\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{t}^{2}\mathrm{I})](x), (63)

and we obtain the following identities:

​C​o​n​d​i​t​i​o​n​a​l​s​c​o​r​e​i​d​e​n​t​i​t​y:∇log⁡pt​(x)=−∫ℝd(x−αt​y)​𝒩​(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑yβt2​∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y,\textstyle\emph{Conditionalscoreidentity:}\qquad\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=-\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(x-\alpha_{t}y)\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{\beta_{t}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}, (CSI)
​T​a​r​g​e​t​s​c​o​r​e​i​d​e​n​t​i​t​y:∇log⁡pt​(x)=∫ℝd∇log⁡pdata​(y)​𝒩​(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑yαt​∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y,\textstyle\emph{Targetscoreidentity:}\qquad\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{\alpha_{t}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}, (TSI)
​N​o​v​e​l​s​c​o​r​e​i​d​e​n​t​i​t​y:∇log⁡pt​(x)=∫ℝd(αt∇logpdata(y)−(x−αty))𝒩(x;αty,β2tI)pdata(y)dy(αt2+βt2)​∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y.\textstyle\emph{Novelscoreidentity:}\qquad\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\alpha_{t}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)-(x-\alpha_{t}y))\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{(\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2})\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}. (NSI)
Proof.

While this result is not new (see Bortoli et al. (2024) and references within), we provide a proof here because of its relevance. Observe that Zt=Xt−αt​Y=βt​ε∼𝒩⁡(0,βt2​I)Z_{t}=X_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y=\beta_{t}\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{t}^{2}\mathrm{I}). The following formula holds for the density of the noised fine-tuned distribution:

pt​(x)=∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖x−αt​y‖22​βt2)(2​π​βt2)d/2​pdata​(y)​dy=∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖x−y~‖22​βt2)(2​π​βt2)d/2​pdata​(y~/αt)​1αt​dy~=∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖x−y~‖22​βt2)(2​π​βt2)d/2​(Tα)#​pdata​(y~)​dy~=[(Tαt)#​pdata∗𝒩⁡(0,βt2​I)]​(x),\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle p_{t}(x)&\textstyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\exp\big(-\frac{\|x-\alpha_{t}y\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)}{(2\pi\beta^{2}_{t})^{d/2}}p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\exp\big(-\frac{\|x-\tilde{y}\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)}{(2\pi\beta^{2}_{t})^{d/2}}p_{\mathrm{data}}(\tilde{y}/\alpha_{t})\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{y}\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\exp\big(-\frac{\|x-\tilde{y}\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)}{(2\pi\beta^{2}_{t})^{d/2}}(T_{\alpha})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}(\tilde{y})\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{y}=[(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}\ast\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{t}^{2}\mathrm{I})](x),\end{split} (64)

where we applied the change of variables y~=Tαt​y=αt​y\tilde{y}=T_{\alpha_{t}}y=\alpha_{t}y, and that the density of the pushforward (Tαt)#​pdata​(x)(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}(x) is pdata​(x/αt)​1αtp_{\mathrm{data}}(x/\alpha_{t})\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}.

Equation (CSI) follows simply from ∇log⁡pt​(x)=∇pt​(x)pt​(x)\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\nabla p_{t}(x)}{p_{t}(x)} and from taking the gradient with respect to xx under the integration sign. We prove (TSI) next. If we let x−αt​y=zx-\alpha_{t}y=z, we have that y=x−zαty=\frac{x-z}{\alpha_{t}}, which implies that |d​yd​z|=1αt|\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}z}|=\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}. Thus, we can write

pt​(x)=∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖z‖22​βt2)(2​π​βt2)d/2​pdata​(x−zαt)​1αt​𝑑z.\textstyle p_{t}(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\exp\big(-\frac{\|z\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)}{(2\pi\beta_{t}^{2})^{d/2}}p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{x-z}{\alpha_{t}})\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}z. (65)

And

∇pt​(x)=∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖z‖22​βt2)(2​π​βt2)d/2​∇x(pdata​(x−zαt))​1αt​𝑑z=∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖z‖22​βt2)(2​π​βt2)d/2​∇x​log⁡pdata​(x−zαt)​pdata​(x−zαt)​1αt​𝑑z=∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖z‖22​βt2)(2​π​βt2)d/2∇logpdata(x−zαt)pdata(x−zαt)1αt2dz=∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖x−αt​y‖22​βt2)(2​π​βt2)d/2∇logpdata(y)pdata(y)1αtdy.\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle\nabla p_{t}(x)&\textstyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\exp\big(-\frac{\|z\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)}{(2\pi\beta^{2}_{t})^{d/2}}\nabla_{x}\big(p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{x-z}{\alpha_{t}})\big)\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}z\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\exp\big(-\frac{\|z\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)}{(2\pi\beta^{2}_{t})^{d/2}}\nabla_{x}\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{x-z}{\alpha_{t}})p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{x-z}{\alpha_{t}})\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}z\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\exp\big(-\frac{\|z\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)}{(2\pi\beta^{2}_{t})^{d/2}}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{x-z}{\alpha_{t}})p_{\mathrm{data}}(\frac{x-z}{\alpha_{t}})\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}z\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\exp\big(-\frac{\|x-\alpha_{t}y\|^{2}}{2\beta^{2}_{t}}\big)}{(2\pi\beta^{2}_{t})^{d/2}}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}y.\end{split} (66)

Using that ∇log⁡pt​(x)=∇pt​(x)pt​(x)\nabla\log p_{t}(x)=\frac{\nabla p_{t}(x)}{p_{t}(x)} concludes the proof of (TSI). To prove (NSI), we sum αt2αt2+βt2\frac{\alpha_{t}^{2}}{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}} times the (TSI) identity and βt2αt2+βt2\frac{\beta_{t}^{2}}{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}} times the (CSI) identity, and obtain:

∇log⁡pt​(x)\textstyle\nabla\log p_{t}(x) =∫ℝd1αt2+βt2(αt∇logpdata(y)−(x−αty))𝒩(x;αty,β2tI)pdata(y)dy∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y.\textstyle=\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}}\big(\alpha_{t}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)-(x-\alpha_{t}y)\big)\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}. (67)

Theorem A.2 (Convolution with a Gaussian Preserves Strong Log-Concavity).

Let f:ℝd→(0,∞)f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(0,\infty) be a density of the form f⁡(x)=e−φ⁡(x)f(x)=e^{-\varphi(x)}, where φ∈C2​(ℝd)\varphi\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfies ∇2φ​(x)⪰γ​I\nabla^{2}\varphi(x)\;\succeq\;\gamma\,I for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, i.e. ff is γ\gamma-strongly log-concave. Let g(x)=(2πσ2)−d/2exp(−‖x‖22​σ2)g(x)\;=\;(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{-d/2}\exp\bigl(-\tfrac{\|x\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\bigr) be the density of 𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I). Define

h=f∗g.h\;=\;f*g.

Then hh is γ1+γ​σ2\displaystyle\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma\,\sigma^{2}}-strongly log-concave, i.e.

∇2[−log⁡h⁡(x)]⪰γ1+γ​σ2​I∀x∈ℝd.\textstyle\nabla^{2}\bigl[-\log h(x)\bigr]\;\succeq\;\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma\,\sigma^{2}}\;I\quad\forall\,x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (68)
Proof.

Set ψ⁡(z)=‖z‖22​σ2\psi(z)=\frac{\|z\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}, F⁡(y,x)=φ⁡(y)+ψ⁡(x−y)F(y;x)=\varphi(y)+\psi(x-y). Then h⁡(x)=∫ℝde−F⁡(y,x)​𝑑yh(x)\;=\;\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{-F(y;x)}\,dy. A standard “log-sum-exp” Hessian identity yields

∇2[−log⁡h⁡(x)]=𝔼⁡[∇x2F​(Y,x)]−Var⁡[∇xF​(Y,x)],\textstyle\nabla^{2}\bigl[-\log h(x)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\nabla^{2}_{x}F(Y;x)\bigr]\;-\;\mathrm{Var}\bigl[\nabla_{x}F(Y;x)\bigr], (69)

where YY is drawn from the density proportional to e−F⁡(y,x)e^{-F(y;x)}. We handle the two terms separately.

1. Second‐derivative term.

∇x2F​(y,x)=∇2ψ​(x−y)=1σ2​I,\textstyle\nabla^{2}_{x}F(y;x)=\nabla^{2}\psi(x-y)=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}I, (70)

so 𝔼⁡[∇x2F]=1σ2​I\mathbb{E}[\nabla^{2}_{x}F]=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}I.

2. Variance term.

∇xF​(y,x)=∇ψ​(x−y)=x−yσ2,\textstyle\nabla_{x}F(y;x)=\nabla\psi(x-y)=\frac{x-y}{\sigma^{2}}, (71)

hence Var⁡[∇xF]=1σ4​Cov​(Y)\mathrm{Var}[\nabla_{x}F]=\frac{1}{\sigma^{4}}\,\mathrm{Cov}(Y).

Since F⁡(⋅,x)F(\cdot;x) is (γ+1/σ2)(\gamma+1/\sigma^{2})-strongly convex in yy, the Brascamp–Lieb inequality gives

Cov⁡(Y)⪯1γ+1/σ2​I=σ21+γ​σ2​I.\textstyle\mathrm{Cov}(Y)\;\preceq\;\frac{1}{\gamma+1/\sigma^{2}}\,I=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{1+\gamma\,\sigma^{2}}\,I. (72)

Therefore,

Var⁡[∇xF]⪯1σ4⋅σ21+γ​σ2​I=1σ2​(1+γ​σ2)​I.\textstyle\mathrm{Var}[\nabla_{x}F]\;\preceq\;\frac{1}{\sigma^{4}}\cdot\frac{\sigma^{2}}{1+\gamma\,\sigma^{2}}\,I=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}(1+\gamma\,\sigma^{2})}\,I. (73)

Combining,

∇2[−log⁡h⁡(x)]⪰1σ2​I−1σ2​(1+γ​σ2)​I=γ1+γ​σ2​I.\textstyle\nabla^{2}[-\log h(x)]\;\succeq\;\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}I\;-\;\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}(1+\gamma\,\sigma^{2})}I=\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma\,\sigma^{2}}\,I. (74)

Thus hh is γ1+γ​σ2\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma\sigma^{2}}-strongly log-concave. ∎

Corollary A.3.

Let ptp_{t} be the density of the marginal X¯t\bar{X}_{t} of the reference flow defined in equation (1). Suppose that the density pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} is in C2​(ℝd)C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and is γ\gamma-strongly log-concave, i.e. −∇2​log​pdata​(x)⪰γ​I-\nabla^{2}\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\;\succeq\;\gamma\,I for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then, for all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], the density ptp_{t} is also in C2​(ℝd)C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and γαt2+γ​βt2\frac{\gamma}{\alpha^{2}_{t}+\gamma\beta_{t}^{2}}-strongly log-concave.

Proof.

By equation (63) from Lemma A.1, we have that

pt​(x)=[(Tαt)#​pdata∗𝒩⁡(0,βt2​I)]​(x),\textstyle p_{t}(x)=[(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}\ast\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{t}^{2}\mathrm{I})](x), (75)

Observe that

∇log⁡[(Tαt)#​pdata​(x)]=∇(Tαt)#pdata(x)(Tαt)#​pdata​(x)=∇x(pdata​(x/αt)​1αt)pdata​(x/αt)​1αt=∇pdata​(x/αt)​1αt2pdata​(x/αt)​1αt=∇log⁡pdata​(x/αt)αt,⟹−∇2​log​[(Tαt)#​pdata​(x)]=−∇2​log​pdata​(x/αt)αt2⪰γαt2​I,\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\nabla\log[(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)]=\frac{\nabla(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}{(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}=\frac{\nabla_{x}\big(p_{\mathrm{data}}(x/\alpha_{t})\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\big)}{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x/\alpha_{t})\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}}=\frac{\nabla p_{\mathrm{data}}(x/\alpha_{t})\frac{1}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}}{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x/\alpha_{t})\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}}=\frac{\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(x/\alpha_{t})}{\alpha_{t}},\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\implies-\nabla^{2}\log[(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)]=-\frac{\nabla^{2}\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(x/\alpha_{t})}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}\succeq\frac{\gamma}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}\mathrm{I},\end{split} (76)

where we used the γ\gamma-strong log-concavity of pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}. This shows that (Tαt)#​pdata(T_{\alpha_{t}})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{data}} is γαt2\frac{\gamma}{\alpha_{t}^{2}}-strongly concave. Thus, a direct application of Theorem A.2 with f=pdataf=p_{\mathrm{data}}, g=𝒩⁡(0,βt2​I)g=\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{t}^{2}\mathrm{I}) implies that the strong log-concavity constant of ptp_{t} is

γ1+γ​σ2=γαt21+γ​βt2αt2=γαt2+γ​βt2.\textstyle\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma\sigma^{2}}=\frac{\frac{\gamma}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}}{1+\frac{\gamma\beta_{t}^{2}}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}}=\frac{\gamma}{\alpha^{2}_{t}+\gamma\beta_{t}^{2}}. (77)

∎

Theorem A.4 (Adaptation of Theorem 2.3 of Shaul et al. (2024)).

Let (αt,βt)(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t}) and (α~r,β~r)(\tilde{\alpha}_{r},\tilde{\beta}_{r}) be two pairs of flow matching coefficients, i.e., differentiable functions αt,α~r:[0,1]→[0,1]\alpha_{t},\tilde{\alpha}_{r}:[0,1]\to[0,1], and αt,α~r:[0,1]→[0,+∞)\alpha_{t},\tilde{\alpha}_{r}:[0,1]\to[0,+\infty) satisfying:

α0=α~0=0=β1=β~1,α1=α~1=1,andSNR(t):=αtβt,SNR~(t):=α~tβ~t are strictly increasing on [0,1).\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\alpha_{0}=\tilde{\alpha}_{0}=0=\beta_{1}=\tilde{\beta}_{1},\quad\alpha_{1}=\tilde{\alpha}_{1}=1,\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\text{and}\ \mathrm{SNR}(t):=\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\beta_{t}},\ \widetilde{\mathrm{SNR}}(t):=\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{t}}{\tilde{\beta}_{t}}\text{ are strictly increasing on }[0,1).\end{split} (78)

B.1 Proof of Prop. 3.1: Bound on the norm of the lean adjoint state

Given a matrix M∈ℝd×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and a point x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the Rayleigh quotient is defined as R⁡(M,x)=⟨x,M​x⟩⟨x,x⟩R(M,x)=\frac{\langle x,Mx\rangle}{\langle x,x\rangle}. The norm of the lean adjoint state a~​(t,Xu)\tilde{a}(t,X^{u}) satisfies the following ODE:

The gradient ∇b\nabla b for 1σ12\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}-strongly convex data distributions

Corollary A.3 proves that when pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} is 1σ12\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}-strongly log-concave, then ptp_{t} is also in C2​(ℝd)C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and 1βt2+αt2​σ12\frac{1}{\beta_{t}^{2}+\alpha^{2}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}}-strongly log-concave. Equivalently, for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1],

−∇𝔰t​(x)=−∇2​log​pt​(x)⪰Iβt2+αt2​σ12,\textstyle-\nabla\mathfrak{s}_{t}(x)=-\nabla^{2}\log p_{t}(x)\succeq\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\beta_{t}^{2}+\alpha^{2}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}}, (115)

which means that

(116)

Observe that this upper-bound matches the right-hand side of (107). Hence, we obtain immediately that for the three subcases, all the equalities involving ∇b​(x,t)\nabla b(x,t) and ∫t1χs​𝑑s\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s become inequalities.

B.2 Derivation of the Target, Conditional and Novel Score Matching loss functions

By the target score identity from Lemma A.1, the density ptp_{t} of the marginal X¯t\bar{X}_{t} of the reference flow in equation (1) satisfies:

∇log⁡pt​(x)=1αt​∫ℝd𝒩(x;αty,β2tI)∇logpdata(Y)pdata(y)dy∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y=1αt​𝔼​[∇log⁡pdata​(Y)|X¯t=x]\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle\nabla\log p_{t}(x)&\textstyle=\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(Y)p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}=\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\mathbb{E}[\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(Y)\,|\,\bar{X}_{t}=x]\end{split} (117)

We use a well-known argument: for any ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued neural network s^\hat{s},

𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)−∇log⁡pt​(X¯t)‖2​𝑑t]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)‖2​dt−2​∫01⟨s^​(X¯t,t),∇log⁡pt​(X¯t)⟩​dt]+const.=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)‖2​dt−2αt​∫01⟨s^​(X¯t,t),𝔼⁡[∇log⁡pdata​(Y)|X¯t]⟩​dt]+const.=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)‖2​dt−2αt​∫01⟨s^​(X¯t,t),∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y)⟩​dt]+const.=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)−1αt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))‖2​dt]+const.\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\nabla\log p_{t}(\bar{X}_{t})\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t-2\int_{0}^{1}\langle\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t),\nabla\log p_{t}(\bar{X}_{t})\rangle\,\mathrm{d}t\big]+\mathrm{const.}\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t-\frac{2}{\alpha_{t}}\int_{0}^{1}\langle\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t),\mathbb{E}[\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(Y)\,|\,\bar{X}_{t}]\rangle\,\mathrm{d}t\big]+\mathrm{const.}\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t-\frac{2}{\alpha_{t}}\int_{0}^{1}\langle\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t),\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\rangle\,\mathrm{d}t\big]+\mathrm{const.}\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]+\mathrm{const.}\end{split} (118)

where the third equality holds by (117). Hence,

ℒTSM​(s^)=𝔼⁡[ℒTSM​(s^,X¯)]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)−1αt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))‖2​𝑑t].\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TSM}}(\hat{s})=\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TSM}}(\hat{s},\bar{X})]=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]. (119)

Analogously to (117), the conditional score identity (CSI) and the novel score identity (NSI) yield

∇log⁡pt​(x)\textstyle\nabla\log p_{t}(x) =−∫ℝd(x−αt​y)​𝒩​(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑yβt2​∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y=−1βt2​𝔼​[x−αt​Y|X¯t=x],\textstyle=-\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(x-\alpha_{t}y)\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{\beta_{t}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}=-\frac{1}{\beta_{t}^{2}}\mathbb{E}[x-\alpha_{t}Y\,|\,\bar{X}_{t}=x], (120)
∇log⁡pt​(x)\textstyle\nabla\log p_{t}(x) =∫ℝd(αt∇logpdata(y)−(x−αty))𝒩(x;αty,β2tI)pdata(y)dy(αt2+βt2)​∫ℝd𝒩⁡(x,αt​y,βt2​I)​pdata​(y)​𝑑y\textstyle=\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\alpha_{t}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)-(x-\alpha_{t}y))\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y}{(\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2})\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_{t}y,\beta^{2}_{t}\mathrm{I})\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y} (121)
=1αt2+βt2𝔼[αt∇logpdata(Y)−(x−αtY)|X¯t=x],\textstyle=\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}}\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{t}\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{data}}(Y)-(x-\alpha_{t}Y)\,|\,\bar{X}_{t}=x], (122)

The expressions for the Conditional Score Matching loss ℒCSM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CSM}} and the Novel Score Matching loss ℒNSM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NSM}} follow from an argument analogous to equation (118), the only differences being that in the second equality we use equations (120) and (122) instead.

B.3 Proof of Prop. 3.2: bias-variance decomposition for Adjoint Matching and Sampling

For Adjoint Matching and Sampling, observe that u⁡(x,t)=12​ηt​(vft​(x,t)−vbase​(x,t))u(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}}\big(v_{\mathrm{ft}}(x,t)-v_{\mathrm{base}}(x,t)\big). Hence,

𝔼⁡[ℒAdj−Match​(u,Xu¯)]=𝔼⁡[12​∫01‖u⁡(Xtu¯,t)+σ​(t)⊤​a~​(t,Xu¯)‖2​𝑑t]=𝔼⁡[12​∫01‖12​ηt​(vft​(Xtu¯,t)−vbase​(Xtu¯,t))+2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)‖2​𝑑t]=(i)𝔼⁡[12​∫01‖vft​(Xtu¯,t)−vbase​(Xtu¯,t)+2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]=𝔼⁡[12​∫01‖vft​(Xtu¯,t)−𝔼⁡[vbase​(Xtu¯,t)−2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)|Xtu¯]‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]+𝔼⁡[12​∫01‖𝔼⁡[vbase​(Xtu¯,t)−2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)|Xtu¯]−(vbase​(Xtu¯,t)−2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯))‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Adj-Match}}(u;X^{\bar{u}})]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\|u(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)+\sigma(t)^{\top}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}}\big(v_{\mathrm{ft}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)-v_{\mathrm{base}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)\big)+\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(i)}}{{=}}\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\|v_{\mathrm{ft}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)-v_{\mathrm{base}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)+2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\|v_{\mathrm{ft}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)-\mathbb{E}\big[v_{\mathrm{base}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)-2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})|X^{\bar{u}}_{t}\big]\big\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\qquad+\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\|\mathbb{E}\big[v_{\mathrm{base}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)-2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})|X^{\bar{u}}_{t}\big]-\big(v_{\mathrm{base}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)-2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big)\big\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\end{split} (123)

Observe that equality (i) yields an expression on the same form as equation (24), with ξ⁡(t,Xu¯)=vbase​(Xtu¯,t)+2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)\xi(t,X^{\bar{u}})=v_{\mathrm{base}}(X^{\bar{u}}_{t},t)+2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}}). The second term in the right-hand side of (123) (the variance term) can be simplified to

𝔼⁡[12​∫01‖𝔼⁡[2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)|Xtu¯]−2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]=𝔼⁡[∫01ηt​‖𝔼⁡[a~​(t,Xu¯)|Xtu¯]−a~​(t,Xu¯)‖2​𝑑t]≤𝔼⁡[∫01ηt​‖a~​(t,Xu¯)‖2​dt]≤∫01ηt​exp⁡(2​∫t1χs​ds)​dt×𝔼⁡[‖∇xr​(X1u)‖2].\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\big\|\mathbb{E}\big[2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})|X^{\bar{u}}_{t}\big]-2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\eta_{t}\big\|\mathbb{E}\big[\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})|X^{\bar{u}}_{t}\big]-\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\leq\mathbb{E}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\eta_{t}\big\|\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\leq\int_{0}^{1}\eta_{t}\exp\big(2\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\,\mathrm{d}t\times\mathbb{E}\big[\|\nabla_{x}r(X^{u}_{1})\|^{2}\big].\end{split} (124)

For the particular case in which pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} is Gaussian, we can similarly obtain an equality:

𝔼⁡[∫01‖𝔼⁡[2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)|Xtu¯]−2​ηt​a~​(t,Xu¯)‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]=𝔼⁡[∫01ηt​exp⁡(2​∫t1χs​ds)​(‖∇xr​(X1u)‖2−𝔼⁡[‖∇xr​(X1u)‖2|Xtu])​dt],\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\mathbb{E}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\big\|\mathbb{E}\big[2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})|X^{\bar{u}}_{t}\big]-2\eta_{t}\tilde{a}(t;X^{\bar{u}})\big\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\eta_{t}\exp\big(2\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\big(\|\nabla_{x}r(X^{u}_{1})\|^{2}-\mathbb{E}\big[\|\nabla_{x}r(X^{u}_{1})\|^{2}|X^{u}_{t}\big]\big)\,\mathrm{d}t\big],\end{split} (125)

where the last equality holds by equation (104). Next, we compute ∫01ηt​exp⁡(2​∫t1χs​𝑑s)​𝑑t\int_{0}^{1}\eta_{t}\exp\big(2\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\,\mathrm{d}t in the three subcases:

  1. (i)

    Föllmer process:

    ∫01ηt​exp⁡(2​∫t1χs​𝑑s)​𝑑t=∫01(σ12(1−α¯t)​σ02+α¯t​σ12)2​α¯˙t​σ022​𝑑t=∫01(σ12(1−t)​σ02+t​σ12)2​σ022​𝑑t=σ122.\textstyle\int_{0}^{1}\eta_{t}\exp\big(2\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}\big(\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sigma_{0}^{2}+\bar{\alpha}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}}\big)^{2}\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}\big(\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{(1-t)\sigma_{0}^{2}+t\sigma_{1}^{2}}\big)^{2}\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{2}. (126)
  2. (ii)

    DDIM/DDPM:

    ∫01ηt​exp⁡(2​∫t1χs​𝑑s)​𝑑t=∫01(σ12​α¯t(1−α¯t)​σ02+α¯t​σ12)2​α¯˙t​σ022​α¯t​𝑑t=∫01(σ12​t(1−t)​σ02+t​σ12)2​σ022​t​𝑑t=σ122.\textstyle\int_{0}^{1}\eta_{t}\exp\big(2\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}\big(\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\sigma_{0}^{2}+\bar{\alpha}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}}\big)^{2}\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}\big(\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}\sqrt{t}}{(1-t)\sigma_{0}^{2}+t\sigma_{1}^{2}}\big)^{2}\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2t}\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{2}. (127)
  3. (iii)

    Rectified Flow:

    ∫01ηt​exp⁡(2​∫t1χs​𝑑s)​𝑑t=∫01(σ12​α¯t(1−α¯t)2​σ02+α¯t2​σ12)2​(1−α¯t)​α¯˙t​σ02α¯t​𝑑t=∫01(1−t)​σ02t​(σ12​t(1−t)2​σ02+t2​σ12)2​dt=σ122.\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\int_{0}^{1}\eta_{t}\exp\big(2\int_{t}^{1}\chi_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}\big(\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}\bar{\alpha}_{t}}{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})^{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}+\bar{\alpha}^{2}_{t}\sigma_{1}^{2}}\big)^{2}\frac{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1-t)\sigma_{0}^{2}}{t}\big(\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}t}{(1-t)^{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}+t^{2}\sigma_{1}^{2}}\big)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{2}.\end{split} (128)

B.4 Proof of Prop. 3.3: bias-variance decomposition for score matching algorithms

Target Score Matching

Next, we write the Target Score Matching and Novel Score Matching losses in the general form (24). Plugging σ⁡(t)=2​ηt\sigma(t)=\sqrt{2\eta_{t}}, we can write

vft​(x,t)=κt​x+2​ηt​s^​(x,t)⟹s^​(x,t)=vft​(x,t)−κt​x2​ηt.\textstyle v_{\mathrm{ft}}(x,t)=\kappa_{t}x+2\eta_{t}\hat{s}(x,t)\implies\hat{s}(x,t)=\frac{v_{\mathrm{ft}}(x,t)-\kappa_{t}x}{2\eta_{t}}. (129)

Thus, for Target Score Matching we have that

𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[12​∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)−1αt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))‖2​(2​ηt)​𝑑t]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[12​∫01‖vft​(X¯t,t)−κt​X¯t2​ηt−1αt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))‖2​(2​ηt)​𝑑t]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[12​∫01‖vft​(X¯t,t)−κt​X¯t−2​ηtαt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[12​∫01‖vft​(X¯t,t)−𝔼⁡[κt​X¯t+2​ηtαt​(∇log⁡pbase​(Y)+∇r​(Y))|X¯t]‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]+𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε[12∫01∥𝔼[κtX¯t+2​ηtαt(∇logpbase(Y)+∇r(Y))|X¯t]−(κtX¯t+2​ηtαt(∇logpbase(Y)+∇r(Y)))∥212​ηtdt]\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}(2\eta_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\frac{v_{\mathrm{ft}}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}}{2\eta_{t}}-\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}(2\eta_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|v_{\mathrm{ft}}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}-\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|v_{\mathrm{ft}}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\mathbb{E}\big[\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)|\bar{X}_{t}\big]\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\qquad+\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\mathbb{E}\big[\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)|\bar{X}_{t}\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad-\big(\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\big)\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\end{split} (130)

The second term in the right-hand side of (130) (the variance term) can be simplified to

𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε[12∫01∥𝔼[2​ηtαt(∇logpbase(Y)+∇r(Y))|X¯t]−2​ηtαt(∇logpbase(Y)+∇r(Y))∥212​ηtdt]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε[12∫012​ηtαt2∥𝔼[∇logpbase(Y)+∇r(Y)|X¯t]−(∇logpbase(Y)+∇r(Y))∥2dt]≤∫01ηtαt2dt×𝔼Y∼pdata[∥∇logpbase(Y)+∇r(Y))∥2].\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\mathbb{E}\big[\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)|\bar{X}_{t}\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad-\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{2\eta_{t}}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}\|\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)|\bar{X}_{t}\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad-\big(\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\leq\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\eta_{t}}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\times\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\big[\|\nabla\log p_{\mathrm{base}}(Y)+\nabla r(Y)\big)\|^{2}\big].\end{split} (131)

Observe that ηtαt2=βt​(α˙tαt​βt−β˙t)αt2\frac{\eta_{t}}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}=\frac{\beta_{t}\big(\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\beta_{t}-\dot{\beta}_{t}\big)}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}. And in particular, for the three subcases:

  2. (ii)

    DDIM/DDPM:

    ηtαt2=α¯˙t​σ022​α¯tα¯t=α¯˙t​σ022​α¯t2⟹∫01ηtαt2​𝑑t=∫01α¯˙t​σ022​α¯t2​𝑑t=+∞\textstyle\frac{\eta_{t}}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}=\frac{\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}=\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2\bar{\alpha}^{2}_{t}}\implies\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\eta_{t}}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{2\bar{\alpha}^{2}_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t=+\infty (133)

    ηtαt2=(1−α¯t)​α¯˙t​σ02α¯tα¯t2=(1−α¯t)​α¯˙t​σ02α¯t3⟹∫01ηtαt2​𝑑t=∫01(1−α¯t)​α¯˙t​σ02α¯t3​𝑑t=∫01(1−t)​σ˙02t3​𝑑t=+∞\textstyle\frac{\eta_{t}}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}=\frac{\frac{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}{\bar{\alpha}^{2}_{t}}=\frac{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\alpha}^{3}_{t}}\implies\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\eta_{t}}{\alpha^{2}_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})\dot{\bar{\alpha}}_{t}\sigma_{0}^{2}}{\bar{\alpha}^{3}_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1-t)\dot{\sigma}_{0}^{2}}{t^{3}}\,\mathrm{d}t=+\infty (134)

Conditional Score Matching

And for Conditional Score Matching, we have that

𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[12​∫01‖s^​(X¯t,t)+X¯t−αt​Yβt2‖2​(2​ηt)​𝑑t]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[∫01‖vft​(X¯t,t)−κt​X¯t2​ηt+X¯t−αt​Yβt2‖2​(2​ηt)​𝑑t]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[12​∫01‖vft​(X¯t,t)−κt​X¯t+2​ηt​(X¯t−αt​Y)βt2‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]=𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[12​∫01‖vft​(X¯t,t)−𝔼⁡[κt​X¯t+2​ηt​(X¯t−αt​Y)βt2|X¯t]‖2​12​ηt​𝑑t]+𝔼Y∼pdata,X¯t=αt​Y+βt​ε​[12​∫01‖𝔼⁡[κt​X¯t+2​ηt​(X¯t−αt​Y)βt2|X¯t]−(κt​X¯t+2​ηt​(X¯t−αt​Y)βt2)‖2​12​ηt​dt].\textstyle\begin{split}\textstyle&\textstyle\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\hat{s}(\bar{X}_{t},t)+\frac{\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y}{\beta_{t}^{2}}\|^{2}(2\eta_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\int_{0}^{1}\|\frac{v_{\mathrm{ft}}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}}{2\eta_{t}}+\frac{\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y}{\beta_{t}^{2}}\|^{2}(2\eta_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|v_{\mathrm{ft}}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}(\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y)}{\beta_{t}^{2}}\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle=\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|v_{\mathrm{ft}}(\bar{X}_{t},t)-\mathbb{E}\big[\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}(\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y)}{\beta_{t}^{2}}|\bar{X}_{t}\big]\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big]\\ \textstyle&\textstyle\ +\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\bar{X}_{t}=\alpha_{t}Y+\beta_{t}\varepsilon}\big[\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\mathbb{E}\big[\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}(\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y)}{\beta_{t}^{2}}|\bar{X}_{t}\big]-\big(\kappa_{t}\bar{X}_{t}+\frac{2\eta_{t}(\bar{X}_{t}-\alpha_{t}Y)}{\beta_{t}^{2}}\big)\|^{2}\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\,\mathrm{d}t\big].\end{split} (135)

And in particular, for the three subcases:
